title: THE PROPHET WHO WAS KILLED BY ANOTHER PROPHET
paragraphs: THE PROPHET WHO WAS KILLED BY ANOTHER PROPHET
There are stories in Scripture that comfort us.
There are stories that inspire us.
And then there are stories that disturb us so deeply that we wish they were not in the Bible at all.
This is one of them.
A prophet of God.
A man who obeyed.
A man sent directly by the LORD.
A man who resisted a king.
A man who stood fearlessly before power.
A man who received clear instructions from heaven.
And then...
He was killed by a lion.
Not because he rejected God.
Not because he worshiped idols.
Not because he committed adultery.
Not because he murdered anyone.
He died because he listened to a prophet who lied.
The story unfolds in 1 Kings 13, and it is one of the most sobering accounts in all of Scripture.
It is a story that begins with courage and ends with tragedy.
But hidden inside the scandal is a message of grace that every believer desperately needs.
Because this is not merely the story of a prophet long ago.
This is the story of every person who has ever struggled to discern God's voice amid the noise of religious voices.
It is the story of every Christian who has ever wondered:
"Who am I supposed to listen to?"

The kingdom of Israel had been torn apart after Solomon's reign. Jeroboam had established false worship in the northern kingdom, creating alternative centers of worship that pulled people away from the LORD.
Into this spiritual chaos, God sent an unnamed prophet.
Scripture calls him simply "a man of God."
The Hebrew expression is אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים (Ish HaElohim) — "Man of God."
His name is never recorded.
His title is.
Because sometimes God wants us to focus more on the mission than the messenger.
Standing before King Jeroboam at Bethel, the prophet boldly pronounced judgment upon the idolatrous altar.
The king was furious.
When Jeroboam stretched out his hand and ordered the prophet's arrest, God's judgment fell instantly.
The king's hand withered.
The altar split apart exactly as the prophet had foretold.
The king suddenly changed his tone.
He begged the prophet to pray for him.
The prophet did.
God restored the king's hand.
What an extraordinary victory.
What faith.
What courage.
What obedience.
Then came the test he never expected.
God had given the prophet explicit instructions.
1 Kings 13:9 records the command:
"Eat no bread, drink no water, and do not return by the way that you came."
No ambiguity.
No confusion.
No mystery.
The command was crystal clear.
The prophet obeyed.
He turned away from the king's invitation.
He rejected royal hospitality.
He refused comfort.
He walked away in obedience.
Had the story ended there, he would have been remembered as one of Scripture's great heroes.
But many spiritual battles are not lost during moments of confrontation.
They are lost during moments of relaxation after victory.
That is where the enemy often waits.
An older prophet heard what had happened.
He pursued the younger prophet.
Eventually he found him resting beneath a tree.
At first the younger prophet remained faithful.
The old prophet invited him home.
The younger prophet refused.
He repeated God's command exactly.
Everything was still safe.
Everything was still clear.
Then the older prophet said something shocking.
"I too am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD."
The Hebrew text records the devastating statement:
כִּחֵשׁ לוֹ
(Kichesh Lo)
"He lied to him."
No misunderstanding.
No miscommunication.
No confusion.
The text explicitly says the old prophet lied.
The younger prophet listened.
And that decision cost him his life.
As they sat eating together, the true word of the LORD finally came.
Judgment was announced.
The younger prophet had disobeyed God's direct command.
When he left, a lion met him on the road and killed him.
What follows is perhaps the strangest detail in the entire narrative.
The lion did not eat the body.
The lion did not attack the donkey.
The donkey stood beside the corpse.
The lion stood beside the corpse.
Both remained there.
A supernatural scene.
A divine sign.
A public testimony.
This was not an accident.
This was judgment.
Yet even here we must be careful.
Many readers walk away from this story believing it is primarily about punishment.
But that misses the deeper point.
Because beneath the tragedy lies a warning wrapped in grace.
The issue was never merely deception.
The issue was abandoning what God had already clearly spoken.
The prophet possessed a direct word from God.
He traded certainty for another voice.
He exchanged revelation for persuasion.
He substituted obedience for approval.
How many believers still do the same?
God speaks clearly through His Word.
Then culture speaks.
Friends speak.
Influencers speak.
Celebrities speak.
Politicians speak.
Experts speak.
Popular teachers speak.
Social media speaks.
Everyone has a voice.
Everyone claims authority.
Everyone claims truth.
Meanwhile many Christians slowly drift from Scripture because another voice sounded convincing.
The Apostle Paul would later warn the church:
"But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed." (Galatians 1:8)
Notice the connection.
The old prophet appealed to angelic authority.
Paul specifically warns believers not to accept messages merely because they appear supernatural.
Truth is not determined by charisma.
Truth is not determined by popularity.
Truth is not determined by spiritual experiences.
Truth is determined by God.
And God never contradicts Himself.
The Greek word Paul uses for gospel is εὐαγγέλιον (Euangelion).
It means "good news."
The good news never changes because the God who gave it never changes.
Yet there is another layer to this story.
A painful one.
The younger prophet's mistake was not rebellion.
It was compromise.
And compromise often disguises itself as sincerity.
Many believers who drift away from God's will are not trying to become evil.
They simply stop guarding the truth God already gave them.
One conversation.
One compromise.
One rationalization.
One exception.
One voice.
That is often all it takes.
Yet remarkably, this story does not end with disgrace.
The older prophet mourned the man he had deceived.
He buried him with honor.
He acknowledged that the younger prophet's original prophecy was true.
Even in death, the word of God stood firm.
The messenger fell.
The message remained.
What a picture of God's sovereignty.
Human failure cannot destroy divine truth.
Human weakness cannot cancel God's purposes.
Human scandal cannot stop God's redemption.
And that brings us to Jesus.
Because every story in Scripture ultimately points toward Him.
Where the unnamed prophet failed, Christ succeeded.
Where the prophet was deceived, Christ resisted every temptation.
Where the prophet listened to another voice, Jesus remained perfectly obedient to the Father's voice.
In the wilderness, Satan repeatedly challenged Him.
Yet Jesus answered every temptation with Scripture.
"It is written."
"It is written."
"It is written."
The first Adam failed.
Israel failed.
Prophets failed.
Kings failed.
We fail.
But Jesus never failed.
The Hebrew concept often translated as obedience is שָׁמַע (Shama).
It means more than hearing.
It means hearing with the intention of obeying.
Jesus perfectly fulfilled what humanity never could.
Philippians 2:8 declares that He became obedient unto death—even death on a cross.
There, at Calvary, another shocking scandal unfolded.
The only truly innocent man in history was executed like a criminal.
The sinless One died for sinners.
The Holy One carried the shame of the guilty.
The King wore a crown of thorns.
The Judge accepted judgment.
The Creator allowed Himself to be crucified by His creation.
And yet through that scandal came grace.
Through that suffering came salvation.
Through that death came life.
This is why our theme remains eternally true:
The unnamed prophet's story warns us never to abandon God's truth.
The Gospel assures us that even when we fail, Christ remains faithful.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to be misled.
Perhaps you trusted the wrong voice.
Perhaps you followed bad counsel.
Perhaps you compromised convictions you once held tightly.
Perhaps your life feels like a collection of mistakes and regrets.
Listen carefully.
Your failures are not greater than Christ's mercy.
Your scars are not stronger than His grace.
Your story is not finished.
The cross proves that God specializes in redeeming broken people.
The empty tomb proves that God can bring life from what appears hopelessly lost.
And if Jesus can transform a cross into a throne and a grave into a victory, He can transform your story too.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
That is the power of grace.
That is why we continue telling these stories.
Not merely to inform minds.
But to awaken souls.
In a world overflowing with confusion, every share becomes an opportunity to point someone toward Jesus Christ.
You may never know how God uses a single conversation, a single article, or a single act of faithfulness to change a life forever.

Your support allows us to create more Gospel-centered articles, discipleship resources, biblical studies, testimonies, and faith-building content designed to lead people from scandal to grace through Jesus Christ.

And before you leave, be honest with yourself:
Whose voice have you been trusting more than God's lately?
Because sometimes the difference between tragedy and transformation is simply returning to the voice that spoke truth from the beginning.
The voice of the Shepherd still calls His sheep by name.
